newsitem.title: CYPRUS: Cyprus dismisses Turkish threats of strike.
newsitem.headline: Cyprus dismisses Turkish threats of strike.

text.p: Cyprus on Friday dismissed a Turkish warning that Ankara would launch an attack if Cyprus went ahead with a plan to deploy anti-aircraft missiles on the island divided between Greek and Turkish communities.

"Every day we are hearing one or two new threats. We are not going to follow the line of Turkey. We are going to concentrate on a political solution to the Cyprus problem," Foreign Minister Alecos Michaelides told Reuters.

Turkish Foreign Minister Tansu Ciller on Friday said the "offensive" Russian S-300 missile system would not be deployed on the island. "If they are deployed we will do what is needed, if that means they need to be hit they will be hit," she said.
Michaelides accused Turkey of stoking tension in the region.

"(Turkish Cypriot leader Rauf) Denktash and Ankara are trying to create tension and discourage countries interested in providing support for a political solution to the problem. We are not going to play their game," the minister added.
Cyprus and Russia signed the missile deal last weekend, drawing criticism from the United States and Britain that the move could scupper peace moves on the militarily divided island.
Both countries have also been critical of Turkish warnings.
Turkish troops have occupied northern Cyprus since 1974, invading days after a short-lived coup in the capital Nicosia inspired by the military rulers of Greece.
Piling the pressure on Cyprus, Denktash threatened to take over Varosha, a Turkish-held resort just south of Famagusta that has been closed off since 1974.
Most of the property in the resort is owned by Greek Cypriots who were forced to abandon their homes there in August 1974 in the second phase of the Turkish invasion.

Cyprus has refused to give in to international pressure to cancel the deal which it says is purely defensive. It says it has the right to protect its inhabitants from a possible Turkish air raid on the southern, Greek populated areas of the island.
"The matter is closed for us," said Michaelides.
Washington is to send an envoy to the island on Sunday to try and reduce the tension. It estimates the system will not be delivered for at least 16 months.

"That is not inaccurate," said Michaelides. "There is at least that much time. There is ample time to solve the Cyprus problem but we need the necessary political will to be displayed by the Turkish side to get down to business."
